analysis.one_liner: Makes federally funded research papers free online within six months of publication.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: introduced May 2006 with bipartisan sponsorship, it never received a hearing or vote before the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill required any federal agency that spends more than $100 million a year on outside research — agencies like NIH and NSF — to post the final, peer-reviewed papers from that research online for free, no later than six months after publication [S2][S3]. It applied both to papers by agency employees and to papers from researchers the agency funds, and excluded books, patentable discoveries, and classified work [S3]. Taxpayers already pay for this research through taxes; today, reading the published results usually means paying a journal subscription or per-article fee [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers who funded the research, plus scientists, physicians, educators, and students who could read the results without paying subscription or per-article fees. Small universities, community colleges, hospitals, and independent researchers without journal subscriptions gain the most, since large research universities already buy access [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and researchers who can't afford journal subscriptions

how_it_helps.text: Requires agencies spending over $100 million on extramural research to create a public access policy making funded, peer-reviewed papers freely available online within six months of publication [S2][S3].

Congress's stated findings were that federally funded research is meant to 'improve the lives and welfare of people of the United States' and that the Internet makes these results available to 'every scientist, physician, educator, and citizen' [S3].
Excludes books, patentable discoveries, and classified research, so it does not strip authors of income from commercial works or undermine patenting [S3].
Requires each agency to report annually to Congress and post publicly on how many funded papers it made accessible and how long each took [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Academic journal publishers, whose business is selling subscriptions and per-article access to papers, would lose some sales when readers can get the free final manuscripts six months after publication. Federal agencies bear the cost of building and maintaining the digital repositories [S3].

drawbacks.text: Journal publishers argued that a short six-month embargo could cut into subscription revenue that funds peer review and journal editing, a real cost an honest supporter would acknowledge.
The bill relies entirely on each agency writing and enforcing its own policy, with only annual reports as a check, so a slow-moving agency could delay compliance with little consequence [S3].
The six-month wait means the newest published findings remain behind paywalls during the embargo period [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is broad and lasting: research paid for with public money becomes readable by the public, which speeds discovery and lets patients, farmers, teachers, and small labs use work they already funded. The cost falls mainly on a small, profitable publishing industry whose subscription model would face pressure — the strongest fair objection is that revenue supports peer review, but the bill preserves publishers' role in it and excludes their most valuable commercial products (books, patents). On balance the benefit to the public outweighs the concentrated cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2006 and referred to the Senate Homeland Security committee, which passed it to a subcommittee and then never acted; the bill died when that Congress ended in January 2007 [S5].

narrative.text: Sen. John Cornyn (R-TX), joined by co-sponsor Sen. Joseph Lieberman, introduced the Federal Research Public Access Act on May 2, 2006 [S1][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs the same day [S5].
On May 26, 2006, the committee referred it to its Subcommittee on Federal Financial Management, Government Information, and International Security, where it stayed [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Journal publishers kept their subscription and pay-per-article revenue from research the public had already paid for, and the agencies' own results stayed behind paywalls.

for.name: Sen. John Cornyn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor [S5].

against.name: Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; its subcommittee held the bill with no hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Federal Financial Management, Government Information, and International Security on May 26, 2006 and took no further action through the end of the Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from introduction — a Republican sponsor and a Democratic co-sponsor (2 co-sponsors total: 1 D, 1 R) [S4] — and it never reached a vote, so no partisan split was ever recorded; the obstacles were inaction in committee rather than party opposition.

industries.note: Publishers sell subscriptions and per-article access to federally funded research; free six-month public access would erode that revenue. Their gain comes from charging people to read work taxpayers already paid for.
Researchers, physicians, and small institutions without big journal budgets would get free access to funded results, which speeds follow-on discovery and citation of their own work.
Their federally funded researchers gain visibility and their libraries save on subscription fees, but they would take on manuscript-submission paperwork under the new policies.
